passage: In the statistics tutorial at her Toronto college, Soo-ah had noticed Leila right away: sharp questions in week one, then silence. By week five, Leila pushed the worksheet away before reading it. "I'm just not a numbers person. I'll fail anyway." Soo-ah had seen her midterm: one early slip had cost her badly, but the reasoning was good. So instead of the full worksheet, Soo-ah slid across a single question, one Leila could solve with what she already knew. "Only this one. Five minutes." Leila sighed and did it. Right. Soo-ah gave her another, slightly harder. Right again. By the end of the hour Leila had done four and was frowning at the fifth by choice. Soo-ah said nothing about it, only ticked the page.

qa.q: What did Leila say when she pushed the worksheet away?
qa.a: "I'm just not a numbers person. I'll fail anyway."

qa.q: Why might Leila have given up before even reading the worksheet?
qa.a: The bad midterm made her believe effort was useless, so not trying felt safer than failing again.

qa.q: Which choice by Soo-ah worked, and why?
qa.a: Giving one question Leila could solve, then slightly harder ones; each success chipped away at the belief that effort changes nothing.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel as Leila frowns at the fifth question by choice?
qa.a: Soo-ah is probably quietly pleased and hopeful, seeing the small steps work, but says nothing so the choice stays Leila's own.

grounding: In a college tutorial, Soo-ah sees a capable student give up in advance and gives her small tasks she can succeed at, which rebuilds effort.

passage: At the polytechnic workshop, Preeti ma'am watched Vijay stand at his bench with his arms folded while the others started on the circuit board. "Why aren't you starting?" "No point, ma'am. Mine never works. Last three boards, all failed." Preeti knew his theory marks were among the best in the class. She also knew how the last three boards had gone: one bad solder each time, and laughter from the next bench when the last one smoked. So she took away the full board and handed him a small strip. "Just solder these four joints. Nothing else." He did it, grumbling. She tested them: perfect. "Now these four." Also perfect. By the end of the session he'd finished the whole power section, and he was the one asking for the next task.

qa.a: A small strip, with four joints to solder.

qa.a: Vijay felt discouraged and embarrassed: three failed boards and the laughter had convinced him his work would fail again, so starting seemed pointless.

qa.q: How might the classmates who laughed see Vijay by the end of the session?

Dear Ujjwal,
I noticed something in class on Monday and wanted to write rather than mention it in front of everyone. When I handed out the essay prompt, you wrote "I can't write essays" at the top of the page and put your pen down. You've said this before. But I've read your lab reports, and they are clear and well argued. So here's my suggestion for this week: don't write the essay. Write only the first paragraph, the one that says what you think and why, and bring it to my office on Thursday. That's all. One paragraph is something I know you can manage. If it goes the way I expect, we'll add the second next week.
Best,
Parveen Qureshi
Lecturer, English Communication

passage: It's small, the thing I'm proudest of this year. I'm Reena, I teach anatomy at a nursing college in Kozhikode, and in the first term I had a student called Yusuf. Lalremsiami Ma'am had taught statistics at the Aizawl college for six years, and she recognised the look.
Eshaan sat in the back row of the first-year class with his arms folded. When she handed out the first problem sheet, he pushed it away without reading it. “I'm just bad at maths, Ma'am. I failed it in Class 12. No point.”

“Bidisha, you haven't started the essay.”
“No point, Ma'am. I'll get a C like always.”
“You got a C once.”
“And a D before that. I'm just not a writer.”
Farida Ma'am sat on the desk beside her. “Okay. Forget the essay. Can you write me one paragraph about the poem's first image? Just one.”

“One. Five sentences.”
Bidisha sighed and wrote. Farida Ma'am read it. “This line, ‘the river forgets its name,’ your point about that is sharp. That's a real insight.”
Bidisha looked up, suspicious. “Really?”

“And then?”
“And then we'll see if you're ‘not a writer.’”
Bidisha looked at the page again. She read her own sentence twice.

passage:
In my first year teaching at the polytechnic, I'm Rafiq, and I met Seema, a second-year electrical student who had stopped trying.
She sat with her textbook closed. In the lab she let her partners do everything. When I asked her about a circuit, she said, “I can't do this, Sir. I've failed two practicals. It doesn't matter what I do.”
But in her first-year file I found a project she'd built: a small solar lamp. It worked. She was capable. She'd just lost the belief that her effort mattered.
So I gave her one simple job: wire a single bulb to a switch. She did it in ten minutes. The bulb lit. I just said, “Good. Next.”
The next week, two bulbs in series. Then a fan regulator.
By the end of term, she was helping her partners. The belief came back slowly, the way a bulb warms up.

qa.q: What project had Seema built in first year?
qa.a: She had built a small solar lamp that worked.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel on finding the solar-lamp project?
qa.a: Rafiq felt encouraged and more determined, seeing that Seema was capable and had only lost belief in her effort.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq's simple tasks work?
qa.a: Each small task was one Seema could succeed at, and the growing successes slowly broke her belief that effort was useless.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt when the first bulb lit?
qa.a: Seema probably felt a flicker of surprise and relief, a first sign her effort could work.

Lecturer's note, first-year statistics — Kalyani
Urmila is one of the sharpest students in the tutorial when we discuss ideas aloud. But whenever a problem sheet appears, she pushes it away before reading it. Today she said, "I'll fail this anyway. I've always been bad at maths." She had not looked at question one.
I did not argue with her. I circled only the first part of question one, finding the mean of five numbers, and asked her to do just that while I walked around the room.
She did it in two minutes, correctly. I said, "That's right," and moved on. When I came back, she had quietly started part two.
It is a small thing. But I think she has had many years of evidence that trying is useless, and she needs fresh evidence that it is not.
Next week: same approach, one small step at a time, slightly harder each time.

Thursday night
Tutorial again. I'm Jatin, the TA for second-year organic chemistry, and today I watched Ayesha close her notebook before I'd even finished writing the problem on the board.
"I can't do mechanisms," she said. "I never could." The thing is, I've seen her answers in the viva. She understands more than she thinks.
I felt frustrated, not with her, with how fast she gave up. So I tried something. I went over and asked her only to draw the first arrow, just the first one, where the electrons move.
She stared at me like I was mad. Then she drew it. Right.
"Now the second?" She drew that too, slower.
By the end she had half the mechanism, and she looked almost annoyed at herself for doing it. I'll try the same thing next week, one arrow at a time.

qa.a: Jatin asked her to draw only the first arrow, where the electrons move.

qa.a: Each arrow was a task small enough to succeed at, so every correct one became evidence against her belief that she couldn't do mechanisms.
